quotes.quote: - **Disease Class**: Mentions that could be described as a family of multiple specific diseases.
- (c) The phrase denotes a family or set: plurals, enumerations, or “types of X” (Section 1.1 and Section 2 apply).

This also covers qualifier spans from Section 1.1 (e.g., “ovarian cancer” in “ovarian cancer cases”), disease names that modify human or clinical nouns (e.g., patients, cases, families, risk, population, phenotype), and disease names in family-history constructions (e.g., “a family history of ovarian cancer”).

note: Rationale also invokes modifying the human noun sister, a second condition in the same sentence.

quotes.quote: For each sentence in the PubMed abstract and title, the locations of all disease mentions are marked, including duplicates within the same sentence.

IF the head noun of a disease mention is a generic category term (e.g., “infection,” “vasculitis,” “deficiency,” or a similar condition-class noun) AND a productive premodifier naming an etiological agent, an anatomical site, or another subtype restricts the phrase so that it denotes one identifiable disease in context, THEN label the entire noun phrase as **Specific Disease**.

IF the head noun of a noun phrase denotes a pathological state or disorder, AND the phrase refers in context to a condition that an organism has or develops (even without a disease-marking word such as “disease” or “syndrome”), THEN label the full phrase as **Disease Class**.
Dependent modifiers, whether anatomical-site adjectives, molecule or substance names, or prepositional complements naming a substance, determine the phrase's extent but not its entity type.
- (a) The head denotes a measured or quantified property (e.g., activity, level, concentration, rate, count), because the phrase then describes a measurement rather than a condition.
- (e) The head is a trait noun (see Clarifications).

note: Rationale calls the duration term 'acute' a dependent modifier; 1.4 lists no duration terms.

quotes.quote: A textual string may refer to two or more separate disease mentions. Such mentions are annotated with the **Composite Mention** category.
- (i) the head is coordinated with, or serves as an umbrella over, several distinct named disorders. These follow the Composite Mention rule in Section 2.

IF the head noun of a noun phrase denotes a pathological state or disorder, AND the phrase refers in context to a condition that an organism has or develops (even without a disease-marking word such as “disease” or “syndrome”), THEN label the full phrase as **Disease Class**.

- **Inheritance-pattern and anatomical-site qualifiers** (e.g., “autosomal recessive,” “X-linked,” “ovarian,” “colorectal”) do not count under (a). “Autosomal recessive disease” therefore remains **Disease Class** (see Example 10).
- (iii) neither (a) nor (b) is present. In that case the standard **Disease Class** criteria apply.

- (e) The premodifier is an inheritance-pattern qualifier (e.g., “autosomal recessive,” “X-linked”), which does not narrow a disease-family head. “Autosomal recessive disease” and “X-linked mental retardation syndrome” remain **Disease Class** (Examples 10 and 12).
- “autosomal recessive disorder” is **Disease Class** (inheritance qualifier only; kind-level statement).

quotes.quote: IF a disease name (full, eponymous, or abbreviated) occurs as a non-final premodifier inside a gene or protein designation, meaning a nomenclature string whose head noun is a molecular term (e.g., “gene,” “protein,” or a numbered variant of these) and which may carry a parenthetical symbol, THEN label the disease substring as **Modifier**. Keep the molecular head noun, index numerals, and parenthetical symbols as O.
